Histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis, and treatment with oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation was initiated. The patient was discharged in stable condition. Key findings include elevated γ-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase levels, normocytic inflammatory anemia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and porto-systemic collateral circulation. Multinodular liver with fibrosis and focal atrophy were confirmed via abdominal CT and biopsy. Mediastinal and hilar adenopathy were noted, along with non-caseating granulomas. The patient’s ACE was raised to 201 UECA, and tuberculin testing and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative. Discharge instructions include continued prednisolone and warfarin therapy, follow-up with primary care and specialist providers, and monitoring for symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

The patient, a 57-year-old male with a history of extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) 3, was discharged following a successful mechanical cardiac support (LCAD) procedure for severe heart failure. The patient received LVAD support for three months, with mediastinal widening noted on a chest X-ray and CT scans revealing mediastinal lymphadenopathy without evidence of disease outside the chest. A pathologic mediastinoscopy was performed, revealing consistent SCLC. The patient was removed from active consideration for cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy was administered while hospitalized, with carboplatin and IV etoposide given. After his first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient chose not to continue it and worked up. Complications included cellulitis, neutropenic fevers with pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and prolonged nausea and vomiting. The treatment course was complicated, with renal function remaining normal, but signs of worsening overload with pleural effusion and peripheral edema developed. The patient elected hospice care and was discharged home, with the patient passing away approximately six months after chemotherapy administration.

Patient: [Patient Name], 72 years, Female, admitted for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Adjuvant systemic therapy with nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor anastrozole (Arimidex®) and CDK 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib (Verzenio®) was administered as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Adjuvant 3D conformal radiotherapy was performed on the right breast and supraclavicular region.  

Following radiation, the patient developed moderate acute radiodermatitis with small moist epitheliolysis in the submammary fold. At completion of RTX, a 2cm wide circumscribed cutis edema at the irradiated area was noted, which later extended to cover the entire irradiated field, with inflammatory infiltrate, hyperpigmentation, induration, and loss of breast volume. A targeted punch biopsy was performed to rule out lymphangiosis carcinomatosa cutis. Histology confirmed no malignant tumor, but dermal fibrosis with thickened dermis and fibrosis extending into underlying tissue was present, along with panniculitis and chronic perivascular inflammation.  

The patient was diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months post-RTX. She declined systemic immune suppression and opted for topical steroids and lymph drainage at a specialized center. The clinical condition remains stable.  

Follow-up instructions: Schedule checkups, monitor affected areas, avoid sun exposure, and apply sunscreen. Discharged with a follow-up care plan. Informed consent provided for follow-up treatment.

Hospital Course: The 29-year-old white male farmer was admitted with left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. On initial examination, splenomegaly was detected, and a high leukocyte count, low hemoglobin level, and high platelet count were noted. Laboratory analysis confirmed CML in chronic phase, and the patient was initiated on hydroxyurea, which was later substituted with imatinib.  

The patient experienced slow progression of splenomegaly until regression occurred within 3 months of imatinib therapy. Initial reevaluation at 3 months showed no symptoms and weight gain, but imatinib was discontinued due to pancytopenia. Bone marrow studies revealed complete remission of CML and numerous Leishmania amastigotes in macrophages. Treatment with pentavalent antimonials was initiated to address leishmaniasis, and the patient achieved complete recovery after 60 days of therapy.  

The patient resumed TKI therapy after acute cardiac toxicity was managed with amphotericin B. A final PCR confirmed deep molecular response. The patient was discharged with good health and recommended for follow-up care.  

Diagnosis: CML in chronic phase, pancytopenia, leishmaniasis, acute cardiac toxicity.

Key findings include a space maintenance orthodontic device between teeth 12 and 14, with clinical exposure of the crown on the palate and three orthodontic buttons for elastic traction. Radiographic exams showed significant bone loss distal to 12 and mesial to 14, with tooth 13 apex constrained within the ennis inverted Y. The patient opted for partial maxillary osteotomy on March 02, 2001, involving the removal of the right canine and a partial osteotomy. Post-surgery, elastic traction was applied to conclude the approximation, with intermaxillary immobilization for 21 days. A continuous arch was used to maintain stability and encourage callus formation. Full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 24, 2001, and the patient was followed up with removable retainers installed by October 23, 2001. The patient requested removal of the internal fixation on October 29, 2010, and clinical and radiographic follow-up confirmed stability and pulpar vitality after 10 years and 10 months of follow-up with excellent periodontal conditions.

Upon admission, the patient had a temperature and was slightly hypoxic. During the physical examination, he was found to have marked jugular venous distension without Kussmaul's sign and pulsus paradoxus. Laboratory results showed significant abnormalities, including reduced white blood cell and neutrophil counts, elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and high lactic acid levels. An electrocardiogram showed normal voltage with diffuse ST-segment elevations. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology and right ventricular collapse in diastole and dilated inferior vena cava. Emergency pericardiocentesis was performed, and 800 mL of green fluid was drained.

The patient was discharged home on the eighth day of hospitalization. He underwent partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear despite an extensive work-up including a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and the chest. The patient was discharged 2 months after discharge and resumed chemo-radiation therapy 2 months after discharge. There was no recurrence of pericardial effusion according to the TTE 4 weeks following discharge.

Admitting Diagnosis: Disproportionate enlargement of right lower limb, abdominal swelling, and growth retardation

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 18-year-old male undergraduate student, presented with a disproportionate enlargement of the right lower limb since the age of 10 years, abdominal swelling for the last 5 years, and growth retardation. He was the first issue from a non-consanguineous marriage and had a normal delivery and normal initial growth spurt that slowed down with adolescence. The patient underwent several evaluations, including physical examination, USG abdomen, and femoral angiography, to establish a diagnosis. Based on the clinical evaluation, the differential diagnosis included Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome, Proteus syndrome, Parkes Weber syndrome, Neurofibromatosis type 1, and Hemihyperplasia-multiple lipomatosis syndrome. Neurofibromatosis type 1 and Hemihyperplasia-multiple lipomatosis syndrome were ruled out due to the absence of stigmata of these diseases. Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome, Proteus syndrome, and Parkes Weber syndrome were considered, and the patient was eventually diagnosed with Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome based on the clinical presentations.

The patient had abnormal body habitus with kyphoscoliosis, left-sided gynecomastia, and gigantic overgrowth of the right lower limb, including toes. His left lower limb was comparatively atrophied. There were multiple nevi distributed predominantly over the right flank, buttock, and right leg with secondary edema, occasional exudation, and eczematous skin changes in the whole of the right lower limb. These epidermal nevi had a mosaic distribution without any cerebriform or gyriform malformation. He also had a huge splenomegaly (15 cm below the costal margin in its axis). The peripheral blood picture revealed trilineage suppression, though bone marrow study was normal. This could be explained by hypersplenism.

On the final evaluation, the patient was found to have only venous malformations with no arterial involvement. Parkes Weber syndrome was ruled out due to the absence of underlying arteriovenous shunts. Klippel-Tre’naunay syndrome was diagnosed as a multicompartment anomaly presenting since birth, characterized by slow flow, mixed capillary venous and lymphatic malformations, and severely affecting the right lower limbs.

Underlying comorbidities, medications, and allergies were not reported in this episode of care.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with no further intervention required.

An 85-year-old Japanese woman with Stage IV squamous cell lung cancer was admitted with rapidly worsening general fatigue and appetite loss eight days after receiving the eighth cycle of pembrolizumab. She had been diagnosed with Stage IV cancer seven months prior. Pembrolizumab was the first-line therapy, resulting in stable disease. Routine examination before each infusion showed no significant changes up to the eighth cycle.

Physical examination revealed no notable findings in head, neck, chest, abdomen, or extremities. No visual deficit was apparent according to the confrontation method.

Laboratory findings included a low serum cortisol level, an inappropriately low ACTH level, hyponatremia with a raised antidiuretic hormone (ADH), and hypoglycemia. Urine osmolarity was elevated despite low plasma osmolarity, indicating inappropriate ADH secretion. There was a poor response to standard-dose short ACTH testing. Serum anti-pituitary cell antibody-1 was negative.

The patient was diagnosed with isolated ACTH deficiency. Hydrocortisone was administered swiftly, which improved her general condition, normalized the ADH level, and corrected the hyponatremia. Adrenal glands were unremarkable on CT. She was discharged and followed monthly in outpatient care. Follow-up showed that cortisol levels ranged from 8.12 to 18.3 μg/dL, while ACTH levels were not detectable during the observation period. ACTH deficiency remained, with no significant changes in thyroid function or other parameters. White blood cell, eosinophil, and electrolyte levels were unremarkable.

An ultrasonography and CT scan were performed, revealing a cystic-like retroperitoneal mass on the left side. Due to persistent pain, a CT-guided puncture was performed, but the cyst was not completely evacuated. Cytology was negative for malignant cells and compatible with a cystic lymphangioma.  

To assess the location of the cyst more precisely, the patient underwent an MRI. T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MR-sequences showed a lesion compatible with a cystic lymphangioma. Due to ongoing symptoms, a surgical resection of this cystic lesion was proposed. The tumor was confirmed to originate from the left adrenal gland, and an "en bloc" left adrenalectomy was performed without rupture. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5.  

Follow-up: The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic one month after the surgery and reported no further symptoms. Histopathology confirmed the final diagnosis of cystic lymphangioma.  

Differential Diagnosis: Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts were considered.  

Treatment: Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for symptomatic cystic lymphangioma. Complete resection of the cyst is recommended, and associated parenchymal resection (adrenalectomy) depends on the location of the cyst and intraoperative dissection.
